section.title: Against Edom and the Mountains Restored
section.sectionRationale: Before the great promises of chapters 36-37 unfold, Ezekiel first turns against Edom, Israel's gloating kinsman-enemy who seized on Jerusalem's disaster to claim her land as spoil. Only once Edom's ancient hatred is judged does the LORD turn to comfort the very mountains of Israel that Edom mocked as desolate and abandoned, promising they will again be tilled, sown, and filled with returning people.
section.thesis: Edom's ancient hatred and gloating claim on Israel's land brings it the same desolation it wished on others, while the mountains of Israel it despised are promised fruitfulness, homecoming, and multiplied life, because the LORD's zeal for His own name and His land will not let either injustice or promise fail.
section.frameNote: Three movements: judgment pronounced against Mount Seir for its ancient hatred and bloodshed; Edom's contemptuous boast against the mountains of Israel turned back on its own head; and the LORD's burning zeal to restore and repopulate the very mountains the nations mocked as desolate.

units.label: Against Mount Seir
units.note: Edom judged for an ancient hatred and bloodshed

verses.text: Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir and prophesy against it,

and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: 
Behold, I am against you, O Mount Seir. I will stretch out My hand against you and make you a desolate waste.

I will turn your cities into ruins, and you will become a desolation. 
Then you will know that I am the LORD.
Because you harbored an {{eybah_olam|ancient hatred}} and delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster at the final stage of their punishment,
therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will give you over to bloodshed and it will pursue you. Since you did not hate bloodshed, it will pursue you.
I will make Mount Seir a desolate waste and will cut off from it those who come and go.
I will fill its mountains with the slain; those killed by the sword will fall on your hills, in your valleys, and in all your ravines.
I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

units.label: Edom's boast against the mountains of Israel

verses.text: Because you have said, ‘These two nations and countries will be ours, and we will possess them,’ even though the LORD was there,

therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will treat you according to the anger and jealousy you showed in your hatred against them, and I will make Myself known among them when I judge you.
Then you will know that I, the LORD, have heard every contemptuous word you uttered against the mountains of Israel when you said, ‘They are desolate; they are given to us to devour!’
You boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me. I heard it Myself!
This is what the Lord GOD says: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate.

As you rejoiced when the inheritance of the house of Israel became desolate, so will I do to you. You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

units.label: The mountains of Israel restored
units.note: reproach reversed, home and fruitfulness promised

verses.text: “And you, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel and say: O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD.
This is what the Lord GOD says: Because the enemy has said of you, ‘Aha! The ancient heights have become our possession,’

therefore prophesy and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Because they have made you desolate and have trampled you on every side, so that you became a possession of the rest of the nations and were taken up in slander by the lips of their talkers,

therefore, O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD. 
This is what the Lord GOD says to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys, to the desolate ruins and abandoned cities, which have become a spoil and a mockery to the rest of the nations around you.

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Surely in My {{qinah|burning zeal}} I have spoken against the rest of the nations, and against all Edom, who took My land as their own possession with wholehearted joy and utter contempt, so that its pastureland became plunder.

Therefore, prophesy concerning the land of Israel and tell the mountains and hills, the ravines and valleys, that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I have spoken in My burning zeal because you have endured the reproach of the nations.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I have sworn with an uplifted hand that surely the nations around you will endure reproach of their own.
But you, O mountains of Israel, will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel, for they will soon come home.
For behold, I am on your side; I will turn toward you, and you will be tilled and sown.
I will multiply the people upon you, the house of Israel in its entirety. The cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt.

I will fill you with people and animals, and they will multiply and be fruitful. I will make you as inhabited as you once were, and I will make you prosper more than before. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
Yes, I will cause My people Israel to walk upon you; they will possess you, and you will be their {{nachalah|inheritance}}, and you will no longer deprive them of their children.
For this is what the Lord GOD says: Because people say to you, ‘You devour men and deprive your nation of its children,’
therefore you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children, declares the Lord GOD.
I will no longer allow the taunts of the nations to be heard against you, and you will no longer endure the reproach of the peoples or cause your nation to stumble, declares the Lord GOD.”

eybah_olam.gloss: Ancient or perpetual hatred, built on the root eybah, enmity, the same word used of the hostility God sets between the serpent and the woman's seed in Genesis 3:15. Edom's grudge against its brother mirrors, in miniature, the deeper enmity running through Scripture's whole story.

qinah.gloss: Zeal or jealousy, the fierce, protective love and anger of a husband defending what belongs to him. Applied here to God's defense of His own land and name against those who mocked and plundered it.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance or possession, the land given to Israel as a lasting family portion. Edom claimed this inheritance for itself, but God insists it belongs to His people alone.

basic.context: Edom, descended from Esau, Israel's own brother, watched Jerusalem fall and moved in on the spoils, saying, 'These two nations and countries will be ours.' Because Edom nursed an ancient hatred and gloated over Israel's disaster rather than showing kinship, God pronounces Mount Seir a perpetual desolation. Then, in the same breath, He turns to comfort the very mountains of Israel the nations mocked as ruined, promising they will again be cultivated, resettled, and filled with His returning people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real, historical judgment on an actual neighboring nation for an actual betrayal (compare the entire book of Obadiah, written on the same theme), paired with a real historical promise of the land's agricultural and demographic restoration after the exile. Its abiding lesson is that gloating over another's downfall, especially a kinsman's, invites the same judgment, while God's zeal for His own name guarantees He will restore what enemies declared beyond hope.
basic.originalLanguages: Edom's crime is named an eyvat olam, an ancient hatred, built on the same root, eybah, enmity, used of the hostility God sets between the serpent and the woman's seed in Genesis 3:15. God's response is described as burning qin'ah, zeal or jealousy, the fierce, protective love a husband has for his wife, aimed here at defending His land's nachalah, its inheritance, from those who despised it.
basic.typology: Edom's judgment for gloating over a brother's disaster answers directly to Obadiah's oracle and anticipates final judgment on all who despise God's people and take pleasure in their downfall, Matthew 25:40-45. The mountains of Israel restored, tilled, and filled with people again anticipate creation itself, groaning under futility, being set free into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, Romans 8:19-21.
basic.christ: Edom stands for every proud enemy that gloats over God's people rather than showing mercy, and its judgment previews the final reckoning for all who do the same, Matthew 25:40-45. But the greater note here is restoration: God's zeal to bring dead land back to fruitful life is the same zeal that raises dry bones in the very next chapter and that, in Christ, reverses the curse on creation itself, Romans 8:19-23.
basic.god: God is zealous, fiercely protective of His own name and His own people, unwilling to let Edom's ancient hatred or the nations' contempt for Israel's ruined mountains go unanswered. He is equally zealous to restore what enemies have declared hopeless, promising fruitfulness and homecoming not because Israel deserves it but because His own reputation and covenant faithfulness are bound up in keeping His word.
basic.crossReferences: Obadiah 1:10-15 addresses the same crime of Edom's gloating and violence against its brother Jacob. Genesis 3:15 shares the same Hebrew root for hatred and enmity. Matthew 25:40-45 shows Jesus applying the same principle to how nations treat His brothers. Romans 8:19-21 previews creation's own coming restoration, foreshadowed here.
basic.oneStory: This is the reckoning before the restoration: Edom's ancient hatred and gloating over Israel's fall is judged, and the very mountains it mocked as desolate are promised fruitfulness and homecoming instead. God's burning zeal for His name will not let contempt for His people or His land have the last word, a pattern that runs all the way to the new creation, where every desolate place is finally, fully restored.

context.literary:
The two oracles are one piece of writing. Chapter 35 is addressed to Mount Seir, and chapter 36 begins with 'And you, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel'. The first speaks against a mountain and the second speaks to mountains, and the whole unit is organised by that pair. Mount Seir is told, 'Behold, I am against you', in 35:3. The mountains of Israel are told, 'I am on your side', in 36:9. The same formula of presence is turned from hostility into favour, and what is done to one mountain range is undone for the other.

Within chapter 35 the structure is a double indictment. Verses 1 to 9 judge Edom for its ancient hatred and for handing Israel over to the sword, and verses 10 to 15 judge it for its boast that the two nations and countries would be Edom's. Each half ends with the knowledge formula, 'Then you will know that I am the LORD', which closes the sections in verses 4, 9 and 15, and verse 11 adds 'I will make Myself known among them'. A noticeable element is the way the sentence mirrors the crime. Edom did not hate bloodshed, so bloodshed will pursue it, verse 6. Edom rejoiced over a desolate inheritance, so it will be a desolation, verse 15.

Chapter 36:1 to 15 reverses the movement. Verses 1 to 7 repeat 'therefore' five times, building a case that the mockery of the nations has been heard. Verses 8 to 12 are a string of promises in the second person to the land itself: branches, fruit, tilling, people, cities, flocks and inheritance. Verses 13 to 15 answer a specific slander, that the land devours its people.

Edom is the sample of the nations. Ezekiel had already issued a short oracle against Edom in 25:12-14, and the full treatment comes here, just before the book's great restoration chapters, so that the enemy who exulted over Israel's ruin is addressed before the ruin is reversed.
context.historical:
Edom was Israel's closest relative. Esau, Jacob's twin, was also called Edom, Genesis 25:30, and he settled in the hill country of Seir, Genesis 36:8. The Torah treated the two peoples as brothers. Moses sent messengers to the king of Edom as 'your brother Israel', Numbers 20:14, Israel was told not to provoke Edom or take its land, Deuteronomy 2:4-5, and not to despise an Edomite, 'for he is your brother', Deuteronomy 23:7. The long record of the two nations was nevertheless one of hostility, from Edom's refusal of passage in Numbers 20:18-21 to its wars with David and the kings of Judah.

When Babylon took Jerusalem in 586 BC, Edom was a bystander who became a participant. Psalm 137:7 remembers the Edomites crying 'Tear it down to its foundations!', Lamentations 4:21-22 tells Edom's daughter that her cup will come, and Obadiah accuses Edom of standing aloof, gloating, looting and cutting off fugitives, Obadiah 1:11-14. Amos had already said Edom 'pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion', Amos 1:11. Ezekiel 35:5 adds that Edom 'delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster'.

Edom's land grab is the likely background to 35:10 and 36:5. With Judah emptied, Edomites and other neighbours claimed its cities and pastures, and Ezekiel quotes them: 'These two nations and countries will be ours' means Israel and Judah, the two kingdoms. In later centuries the Edomites were pushed westward into the territory south of Judah that came to be called Idumea, and by the New Testament period people from Idumea were among those coming to Jesus, Mark 3:8.

The 'mountains of Israel' were a real geography of terraced hills, vineyards and sheep pasture. After the fall, the hill country lay depopulated, and neighbours called it 'the ancient heights', 36:2, which may be a taunt that the old high places of Israel now belonged to them.
context.canonical:
The story of Edom is the story of a family quarrel that never closes. It begins in the womb, where God tells Rebekah that 'the older will serve the younger', Genesis 25:23, and it includes the stolen blessing and the vow of revenge, Genesis 27:41. There is a moment of reconciliation in Genesis 33:4, when Esau runs and embraces Jacob, which makes the later enmity harder to read. Malachi 1:2-4 looks back on the whole relationship and says God loved Jacob and set Esau's mountains in ruins, and Paul draws on the verse in Romans 9:13.

The prophets use Edom as the pattern of a hostile neighbour. Isaiah 34 and 63:1-6 picture the LORD's judgment as a slaughter in Edom's chief city, Bozrah, and Jeremiah 49:7-22, Joel 3:19 and the whole of Obadiah speak to the same effect. Because the same crime is named so often, Edom comes to stand for everything that revels in the fall of God's people. Proverbs 24:17-18 gives the moral rule behind it: 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls.'

The restoration side of the passage belongs to a wide stream of promise. Isaiah 51:3 says the LORD will make Zion's wilderness like Eden, Isaiah 61:4 says the ancient ruins will be rebuilt, Isaiah 49:19-20 pictures a land too small for its returning people, and Isaiah 62:4 says the land will no longer be called Desolate. Zechariah 1:14-15 and 8:2 repeat the language of jealousy for Zion that appears in 36:5 and 6.

In the New Testament, Jesus applies the principle of Edom's judgment to the nations in Matthew 25:40 and 45, where what is done to His brothers is done to Him. Paul extends the land promise to the world when he says Abraham and his offspring were to be 'heir of the world', Romans 4:13, and Jesus says the meek 'will inherit the earth', Matthew 5:5. Romans 8:19-21 reads creation itself as waiting for its deliverance.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's first purpose is to answer a charge against God's character. The nations looked at ruined Israel and drew a conclusion, either that its God was weak or that He had abandoned His land. Edom said so openly: 'They are desolate; they are given to us to devour!' The prophet is told to answer on God's behalf. The LORD heard every word, 35:12 and 13, and an insult to the people of the covenant is an insult to Him. The opening claim in verse 10, 'even though the LORD was there', says that Edom treated His presence as nothing.

The second purpose is to give the exiles a reason to look at their devastated land with hope. The mountains they remember, now overgrown and mocked, are addressed by God, who calls them to hear His word. The promise of verses 8 to 12 is that the land will be tilled, the cities rebuilt, the people multiplied, and that the people who come will find a land that no longer devours but nourishes. For a hearer in Babylon the message is that the place he grieves for is still on God's heart and will be given back.

A third purpose is moral. Edom's guilt is not that it was an enemy but that it delighted in a brother's ruin. The passage tells Israel and any reader to take the stance opposite to Edom's: mourn with the one who falls, and do not take advantage. It also tells Israel that its future does not depend on its own strength but on God's zeal, since the repeated 'therefore' of chapter 36 makes the mockery of the nations the ground of His action.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a specific judgment on a specific nation and a specific promise to a specific land. It does not tell the modern church to treat any present nation as Edom, and it gives no licence to cast a political enemy in that role. Edom's sentence is tied to what Edom did, namely harbouring ancient hatred, delivering over the fugitives, and claiming the land, and it came from God, not from Israel's own hand.

The sentence on Edom does set a principle that holds in any age: God hears what people say about His own, and gloating over the downfall of others is an offence He answers. Proverbs 24:17-18 and Romans 12:15 give the ethical form. Believers are called to weep with those who weep and not to rejoice when an enemy falls.

The restoration promises need equal care. They were made to Israel in exile about a physical land and were first fulfilled in the return from Babylon, but they are also taken up in the New Testament as pointing to the larger inheritance of Christ's people. The principle that carries over is that God's promises of restoration are as solid as His judgments, and that He acts for His name's sake, as the next chapter says, not because the recipients are deserving.

debates.question: Is Edom here a historical nation only, or also a symbol of all the nations hostile to God?

views.label: A historical nation
views.case: The oracle names Mount Seir and all of Edom, 35:2 and 35:15, and the crime is specific: it handed Israel to the sword at the final stage of their punishment and claimed their land. Obadiah, Psalm 137:7 and Lamentations 4:21-22 describe the same events. On this view the prophecy was fulfilled in the later decline of Edom and the loss of its territory.

views.label: Both a nation and a representative of the nations
views.case: The statement in 36:5 that God has spoken 'against the rest of the nations, and against all Edom', and the phrase 'While the whole earth rejoices' in 35:14 widen the frame. Isaiah 34 and 63:1-6 also use Edom as the place where God's final judgment falls. Many readers see in Edom a type of the world that rejoices in the harm done to God's people.

debates.bearing: The two readings are compatible. The oracle begins with a real nation and a real crime, and the New Testament teaches that how the world treats Christ's people is how it treats Him, Matthew 25:40 and 45, and Acts 9:4. Using Edom as a pattern should not make us forget it was first a historical judgment on a neighbour.

debates.question: In what sense are the promises of 36:8 to 12 fulfilled?

views.label: In the return from Babylon
views.case: Cyrus's decree sent exiles home from 538 BC, Ezra 1:1-4, and the cities were rebuilt and farmed again. Verses like 'they will soon come home', 36:8, fit that near horizon. A strict reading holds that the prophecy was fulfilled in the post-exilic community, though some of its language went beyond what that community experienced.

views.label: Partly then, finally in Christ and the new creation
views.case: The promise that the land would be more prosperous than before, 36:11, and that it would never again bereave the nation, 36:12 to 15, was not fully realised in the second temple period. The New Testament extends the inheritance to the world, Romans 4:13, and sees creation set free, Romans 8:19-21. On this view the return is a first instalment, and the Eden language of the next chapter points to the end.

views.label: A future restoration of Israel in its land
views.case: Another view, held by many dispensational and some other interpreters, expects a yet future regathering of Israel to the land, in line with Romans 11:26-29 and the repeated promises of the prophets. It reads 36:8 to 12 as awaiting that event.

debates.bearing: Each view accepts that God keeps His promises to the land and the people. The text itself stresses the cause, His zeal and His sworn word, 36:5 to 7, more than the timetable. Readers are wise to hold the question of fulfilment with humility while holding firmly to the character of the God who promises.

study.originalLanguages:
The first charge against Edom is that it harboured an 'ancient hatred', eyvat olam, in 35:5. The word eyvah is the noun for enmity, and it is the same one God places between the serpent and the woman in Genesis 3:15. In Numbers 35:21-22 it marks the hatred that separates a murderer from an accident. The adjective olam means 'long ago' or 'lasting', so Edom's hostility is an inherited grudge nursed across generations, and Ezekiel 25:15 uses the same phrase of the Philistines' old hostility toward Judah. The family root goes back to Genesis 27:41, where Esau resolves to kill Jacob.

Verses 5 and 6 play on sound. The word for blood, dam, is almost the name Edom, and the sentence 'I will give you over to bloodshed and it will pursue you' puts the two side by side. Edom's name also meant 'red', Genesis 25:30, so the ear catches a word-play on a nation named for the colour of the very thing that will consume it. The reason given, 'you did not hate bloodshed', shows that the guilt lies in a settled attitude as well as in deeds.

The phrase 'at the final stage of their punishment' in verse 5 is the one used of Israel's last prince in 21:25. It marks the moment when Jerusalem's fate was already sealed and Edom, rather than showing mercy, struck. Verse 10 adds a short clause with great weight in Hebrew, 'even though the LORD was there', which is echoed in the closing line of the whole book, where the city is named 'THE LORD IS THERE', 48:35. Edom took the land as though its owner were absent.

Chapter 36 uses the word qinah, zeal or jealousy, twice in verses 5 and 6, in the phrase translated 'burning zeal'. The verb is the one that stands behind the description of God as a 'jealous God' in Exodus 20:5. It is the passion of a love that will not share or see harm come to what it loves, and in 5:13 the same word marks the zeal in which God speaks judgment on Israel itself. Here the target is outward, and the zeal is aimed at those who trample His people. In 39:25 the same word describes God's jealousy for His holy name.

The word nachalah, inheritance, in 35:15 and 36:12, belongs to the vocabulary of the land. Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard because it is 'the inheritance of my fathers', 1 Kings 21:3, and the land is God's gift to families that cannot be alienated. When Edom rejoices over 'the inheritance of the house of Israel', it is rejoicing over God's own gift. When God says the mountains will be Israel's inheritance again, He restores the ordering of the promise.

The slander in 36:13 that the land 'devours men' and 'deprives your nation of its children' echoes the spies' report that the land 'devours its inhabitants', Numbers 13:32. Two of the verbs the passage uses for the mountains' restoration in 36:8 and 9, 'branches' and 'tilled and sown', are agricultural, and the plain promise of fruit is notable: the land that was said to eat its people will feed them. The turn between 35:3 and 36:9 is made in English by 'I am against you' and 'I am on your side', one formula with its meaning reversed.

typology.fulfillment: Esau's line stands for the relative who stands aloof or rejoices when God's people fall, and its judgment prefigures the final reckoning of all who do so. Jesus makes the link in Matthew 25:40 and 45, where care or neglect of His brothers is care or neglect of Him, and He asked Saul on the Damascus road, 'why do you persecute Me?', Acts 9:4. Edom's story also carries a lesson for the church, since Paul warns believers not to rejoice at another's fall, Romans 12:15, and 1 Corinthians 13:6 says love does not rejoice at wrongdoing. The type falls short because Edom's sentence was historical and the final judgment is spoken by Christ.

The mountains, hills, ravines and valleys of 36:4 are addressed as though they could hear, and are told a word of comfort that the mockers did not hear. The pattern of a ruined place being addressed by God and promised life looks forward to the creation that groans and waits to be set free, Romans 8:19-21. In Christ the pattern is realised, since all things are reconciled to God through Him, Colossians 1:20, and the new creation is a place where the former things have passed away, 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Revelation 21:1. The type is limited to a land, and the fulfilment reaches the whole earth.

The mountains that will again be Israel's inheritance, 36:12, point to a larger inheritance. Abraham looked for a city whose builder is God, Hebrews 11:8-10, and Paul says he was to be 'heir of the world', Romans 4:13. Jesus promises that the meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and Peter speaks of an inheritance that is imperishable, 1 Peter 1:4. The type is bounded by borders and by the possibility of loss, as the exile showed, while the inheritance in Christ is kept in heaven and cannot be lost.

The shift from 'I am against you' in 35:3 to 'I am on your side' in 36:9 shows the shape of the gospel. For those who persist in hatred the first stands, and for those who are His the second becomes true. Paul says 'If God is for us, who can be against us?', Romans 8:31, and he grounds it in the fact that God gave His Son, Romans 8:32. In Christ the face that was against sin turned toward sinners, and the cross is where the two meet. The type is incomplete, because the mountains did nothing and needed nothing, while sinners must be reconciled.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by showing what stands against God's people and what God does about it. Edom's attitude, delight in the downfall of a brother, is the old enmity of Genesis 3:15 in political form, and that enmity is the thing Christ came to end. At the cross He took the judgment that Edom's spirit deserves and offered its opposite, forgiveness for those who mocked Him, Luke 23:34. The pattern of Mount Seir is turned inside out when the one who is gloated over, 'He saved others; let Him save Himself', Luke 23:35, prays for the mockers.

The identification of Christ with His people gives the oracle sharper edges in the New Testament. When Jesus says that what is done to the least of His brothers is done to Him, Matthew 25:40, He claims for Himself the place Israel held in Ezekiel 35, as the one whom the world's hostility strikes. Saul learns the same on the road to Damascus, Acts 9:4. The sentence of 35:11, that God will 'treat you according to the anger and jealousy you showed', sets a measure that Jesus repeats in the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:2.

The second half of the passage leads to Christ by the shape of its hope. The land will be given back, but not because Israel has deserved it. The ground is God's zeal and His oath, 36:5 to 7. In Christ that oath is ratified, since all the promises of God find their 'Yes' in Him, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The inheritance the mountains stand for becomes the inheritance of the world, and the land that was said to devour its inhabitants gives way to the kingdom prepared for the blessed, Matthew 25:34.

The promise that the desolate land will be tilled and sown, and the people multiplied upon it, is also the pattern of resurrection. Ruined places returning to life belongs to the same set of images as the dry bones of the next chapters, and Christ is the one who gives life to the dead, John 11:25. Creation's restoration is bound to His, Colossians 1:20 and Romans 8:21. A word of care: the passage does not name the Messiah, and it is wiser to say that its themes of enmity, zeal, inheritance and restoration are the themes the New Testament shows fulfilled in Christ than to read every detail of Edom or the mountains as a hidden picture of Him.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who hears. 'I heard it Myself!' in 35:13 is among the most striking sentences in the chapter. The boasts Edom made when no one from Israel was listening reached the ears of the LORD, and 36:3 says the mountains were taken up in the slander of the talkers, so the reproach of the nations is on His record as well. Nothing said against His people is said in secret. That is a comfort to those who are mocked and a warning to those who mock.

It also shows a God who is personally invested in a place and a people. He says 'My land', 'My people Israel', and 'My name' in the same breath. The zeal He speaks with, 36:5 and 6, is the passion of a husband or a father defending what is his, and He says the fire of it is the reason for the oracle. This is not the temper of a deity who is indifferent to human affairs. It is the energy of a covenant partner who acts when the covenant is trampled.

The chapters hold two truths together. God is just toward Edom, and the sentence mirrors the crime, with bloodshed answering a lack of hatred for bloodshed, and desolation answering rejoicing over desolation. And God is generous toward Israel, who had been judged for sins of its own, in giving back the land beyond what it had before, 36:11. The justice is not softened and the mercy is not earned. Both come from the same character, which the next chapter states plainly: He acts for His holy name.

The wording 'I am against you' and 'I am on your side' shows God's freedom to set His face. He can be on one side or the other of any people, and He does not do so from favouritism but from faithfulness to His word. The same God who tells Rebekah that the older will serve the younger, Genesis 25:23, who gave Edom its own mountain, Deuteronomy 2:5, and who commanded Israel to treat Edom as a brother, judges Edom for what it did to a brother.

For worship, these chapters invite praise for a God who vindicates. They teach us to bring the insults, the slanders and the ruins to Him rather than avenge them, Romans 12:19. And they give us language to pray, as the psalmist does in Psalm 137:7, for the Lord to remember, trusting that He has heard.

crossReferences.note: The sharpest parallel in the Bible to Ezekiel 35. Obadiah lists Edom's offences in the day of Jerusalem's fall: standing aloof, gloating, looting and blocking the fugitives. The two prophets agree on the crime and its sentence, and reading them together fills out what 'delivered the Israelites over to the sword' meant in practice.

The exiles' own memory of what Edom said on the day Jerusalem fell: 'Tear it down to its foundations!' It gives a voice to the contempt Ezekiel reports in 35:12 and shows why the memory still hurt in Babylon. The psalm prays for God to remember, and Ezekiel 35 is the answer that He has.

The origin of the two nations in the womb of Rebekah and the sale of the birthright for red stew, which gives Esau the name Edom. The oracle's wordplay on blood and Edom has its root here, and the story shows how deep the family line of the enmity runs.

The command 'Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother' shows what Edom owed Israel and what Israel owed Edom. The fault in Ezekiel 35 is therefore a breach of kinship, and not the ordinary hostility of strangers. It also shows that the Torah's treatment of Edom was kinder than the way Edom treated Israel.

The wisdom saying behind the oracle: 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls.' The proverb warns that the LORD sees and disapproves, which is just what Ezekiel 35:12 and 13 say about Edom's boasting. It turns a prophetic sentence into a rule for personal life.

The spies' bad report that the land 'devours its inhabitants'. Ezekiel 36:13 quotes the old slander that the land eats its people and promises that it will no longer do so. The land that frightened the first generation is turned into one that nourishes the last.

The LORD will comfort Zion and 'make her wilderness like Eden'. It supplies the language that the next section of Ezekiel uses in 36:35, and it shows that the promise to the mountains of Israel belongs to a larger prophetic vision of the renewal of the earth.

God says He is jealous for Zion 'with great zeal'. It uses the same family of words as the 'burning zeal' of Ezekiel 36:5 and 6, and shows that the passion that judges Israel's enemies is the one that guards the city after the return.

Jesus teaches that what is done to the least of His brothers is done to Him. This is the New Testament form of the principle in Ezekiel 35, where an insult to Israel is heard as an insult to the LORD, and it shows that the principle widens to all who belong to Christ.

Creation waits in eager expectation to be set free from bondage to decay. The mountains addressed by Ezekiel are an early picture of that hope, and Paul places it at the end of the story. The promise to the land becomes a promise to all of creation.

'If God is for us, who can be against us?' is the New Testament counterpart to 'I am on your side' in Ezekiel 36:9. The God who set His face against Edom set it for His people, and Paul roots the confidence in the gift of His Son.

study.oneStory:
The enmity Genesis 3:15 puts between the serpent and the woman's seed has a long human history, and Edom is one of its recurring faces. The war runs through the twin sons of Isaac, through Amalek and Pharaoh and Haman, and it appears here as a brother who watches Jerusalem burn and says, 'It is ours.' The chapters read as a chapter in the story of that war, and they show that God does not forget what is done to His people. Cain, who killed a brother, is the first picture of the pattern, Genesis 4:8, and Edom is a nation that took that path.

The chapters also take up the story of the land. In Genesis 15:7 God gives Abraham a land to possess, in Joshua it is divided, and in Leviticus 18:24-28 it is said that the land will vomit out those who defile it. Ezekiel stands at the point where that warning has come true, and the land is empty and mocked. The question is whether the promise to Abraham has ended. The answer, in 36:8 to 12, is that it has not, and that the land will be tilled again, because the promise rests on God's word and not on the people's record.

This is the first of three movements that carry the book through its second half. Chapter 35 and 36:1 to 15 judge the enemy and restore the land, 36:16 to 38 deal with the people's hearts, and chapter 37 raises the dead nation and makes it one. The land comes first because it was the visible sign of the covenant, and the order tells us God restores the whole of what He made, not only souls.

The New Testament carries the promise in two directions. It widens the inheritance, since Abraham is heir of the world and the meek inherit the earth, Romans 4:13 and Matthew 5:5, and it looks to a creation set free from decay, Romans 8:21. The story ends in Revelation 21 and 22, where there is a new heaven and a new earth, the nations walk by the light of the city, and there is no longer any curse. Edom's kind of hatred has no place there. The ruined places are not simply mended. They are replaced by a garden city with the tree of life on both sides of its river, Revelation 22:2, and the name that Ezekiel gave the city at the end of his book, THE LORD IS THERE, is the last word.

quiz.q: What specific charge does God bring against Mount Seir (Edom) in 35:5?

options.text: They harbored an ancient hatred and delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster.
options.note: Verse 5 states this exact charge, an ancient hatred acted on at Israel's moment of greatest need.

options.text: They refused to pay tribute to Israel's king.
options.note: No mention of tribute appears; the charge concerns hatred and violence, not taxation.

options.text: They built idol shrines on Israel's mountains.
options.note: The charge is betrayal and bloodshed against Israel in disaster, not idol construction.

options.text: They invaded Israel's territory with a standing army.
options.note: The charge is about delivering Israelites to the sword and opportunistic gloating, not a formal invasion.

quiz.q: What specific claim does Edom make about Israel's land in 35:10 and 36:2?

options.text: That these two nations and the ancient heights will become their own possession, even though the LORD was there.
options.note: Both verses record this exact claim of possession over Israel's territory.

options.text: That Israel had forfeited the land through an unfair treaty.
options.note: No treaty dispute is mentioned; the claim is a direct assertion of ownership by conquest opportunity.

options.text: That the land legally belonged to Assyria rather than Israel.
options.note: Edom claims the land for itself, not on behalf of Assyria.

options.text: That the land should be left uninhabited by anyone.
options.note: Edom explicitly wants to possess and devour the land, not leave it empty.

quiz.q: How does God answer Edom's gloating over Israel's disaster, 35:15?

options.text: As Edom rejoiced over Israel's ruin, so God will do to Edom, making it a desolation.
options.note: Verse 15 states this direct measure-for-measure judgment plainly.

options.text: God ignores Edom's words as unimportant.
options.note: The opposite is true; God says explicitly, 'I heard it Myself!' verse 13.

options.text: God rewards Edom's boldness with expanded territory.
options.note: God pronounces desolation on Edom, not reward, verse 15.

options.text: God asks Israel to make peace with Edom immediately.
options.note: No call to reconciliation appears here; the passage pronounces judgment on Edom.

quiz.q: What does God promise the mountains of Israel in 36:8-11?

options.text: They will produce branches and fruit for God's people, be tilled and sown, and be filled with multiplying people and animals.
options.note: Verses 8-11 detail exactly this fruitfulness, cultivation, and repopulation.

options.text: They will remain desolate forever as a permanent memorial.
options.note: The opposite is promised: full restoration to fruitfulness and habitation.

options.text: They will be given entirely to the surrounding nations to farm.
options.note: The mountains are promised to God's own people Israel, not to the surrounding nations, verse 8.

options.text: Nothing specific is promised to the mountains themselves.
options.note: Very specific promises are given directly to 'the mountains of Israel' by name throughout this section.

quiz.q: According to 36:5-6, why is God's judgment against Edom and the nations described as coming from His 'burning zeal'?

options.text: Because they took His land with wholehearted joy and utter contempt, making its pastureland their plunder.
options.note: Verse 5 states this cause explicitly as the reason for God's burning zeal.

options.text: Because they refused to worship at Jerusalem's temple.
options.note: The stated reason concerns contemptuous seizure of the land, not a worship dispute.

options.text: Because they were more militarily powerful than Israel.
options.note: Military strength is not the stated cause; contemptuous seizure of God's land is.

options.text: No reason is given for God's zeal in this passage.
options.note: A specific, clearly stated reason is given directly in verse 5.

questions: Edom's sin was gloating over a brother's disaster instead of showing mercy. Where might you be tempted to feel quiet satisfaction when someone who has wronged you or competed with you falls on hard times?

God calls Edom's hostility an 'ancient hatred', a grudge nursed over time rather than a single outburst. Is there a long-held resentment you are still nursing that this passage calls you to finally release?

God promises to restore mountains that the nations declared permanently desolate and beyond hope. What situation in your life feels like a 'desolate mountain' that you've stopped believing God could restore?

The whole point of God's zeal here is that His name and reputation are bound up with keeping His promises to His people. How does it change your confidence to know God's restoration of you is motivated by His own faithfulness, not by whether you've earned it?

Creation itself groans for the same kind of restoration promised to these mountains, Romans 8:19-21. Where do you most need to hold onto hope that God is still in the business of making desolate, hopeless places fruitful again?

translationNotes.note: 'Mount Seir' is the mountainous region south and east of the Dead Sea, the territory of Edom, so the name functions here as shorthand for the whole nation, much as 'Zion' can stand for Jerusalem or Israel.

'Ancient hatred' translates a Hebrew phrase (eyvat olam) built on the same root, eybah, rendered 'enmity' in Genesis 3:15, linking Edom's grudge against its brother to the deeper pattern of hostility running through Scripture's story.

'Burning zeal' (qin'ah) can also be rendered jealousy; the Hebrew word describes the fierce, protective love and anger of a husband defending what belongs to him, applied here to God's defense of His own land and name.
